items.answer: A LAN covers a small area (a school) and is usually owned by one organisation; a WAN covers large areas (countries) and connects many LANs, often using leased or public infrastructure.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Cloud computing has made organisations more resilient."
items.answer: The cloud improves resilience for many individual organisations but concentrates systemic risk in a few providers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: redundant data centres and professional security; scales instantly to demand. Arguments against: concentration on a few providers creates single points of failure (AWS 2021, CrowdStrike 2024); dependence on network connectivity; vendor lock-in. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Everyone needs to understand how the internet works to be a responsible digital citizen."
items.answer: A basic understanding is valuable for safety and civic debate, but secure-by-default design matters more than individual expertise.

items.answer: Packets from many users share the same links, using capacity efficiently; if a route fails, packets can be re-routed, making the network resilient – a design goal of ARPANET.

items.stem: Using the Facebook outage of October 2021 as an example, explain protocols and routing.
items.answer: On 4 October 2021 a faulty configuration change to Facebook's BGP routing withdrew routes to its DNS servers, taking Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp offline for about six hours. When routing announcements disappeared, the rest of the internet could not find Facebook's servers, showing how services depend on protocols working correctly.

items.answer: Systems that tolerate small variations in others' messages while sending strictly correct ones can interoperate despite differences, enabling diverse networks to connect.

items.stem: With reference to the Mirai botnet attack (2016), explain how it illustrates security risks of the Internet of Things.
items.answer: In October 2016 the Mirai botnet, made of hacked IoT cameras and routers with default passwords, launched a massive DDoS attack on DNS provider Dyn, disrupting major websites in the US and Europe. Insecure everyday devices became weapons, showing that the security of the whole network depends on its weakest connected things.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the whole web and a search engine index.
items.answer: An index is the search engine's database of pages its crawlers have found and processed; much of the web (private, dynamic or blocked pages – the "deep web") is not indexed.
items.markingKey: An index is the search engine's database of pages its crawlers have found and processed; much of the web (private, dynamic or blocked pages – the "deep web") is not indexed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a WAN and a LAN.
items.answer: A LAN covers a small area (a school) and is usually owned by one organisation; a WAN covers large areas (countries) and connects many LANs, often using leased or public infrastructure.
items.markingKey: A LAN covers a small area (a school) and is usually owned by one organisation; a WAN covers large areas (countries) and connects many LANs, often using leased or public infrastructure. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between TCP and IP.
items.answer: IP is responsible for addressing and routing each packet to the destination; TCP manages the connection, splitting data into packets, numbering them, checking delivery and resending lost packets.

items.stem: A small office network has a 1000 Mbps connection to the internet shared equally by 40 active users. Calculate the bandwidth available to each user.
items.answer: 25 Mbps

items.stem: A fibre-optic cable route from London to New York is about 5,600 km long. Light travels through optical fibre at about 200,000 km/s. Calculate the minimum one-way delay in milliseconds and the round-trip time.
items.answer: 28 ms one way; 56 ms round trip

items.stem: An estimated 10 billion IoT devices were connected in 2022. If the number grows by 12% a year, estimate the number connected in 2026. Explain one security risk created by this growth.
items.answer: about 15.7 billion; many devices have weak default passwords and are rarely updated, so they can be hijacked into botnets (e.g. Mirai, 2016)
items.markingKey: 10 × 1.12^4 [M1] = 15.7 billion [A1]. Weak defaults/no updates → botnets such as Mirai (2016 Dyn DDoS) [R1 R1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which the AWS outage of December 2021 shows interdependence in cloud networks.
items.answer: An outage in Amazon Web Services' US-East-1 region disrupted services such as Disney+, Ring doorbells and delivery apps. Many services relied on the same cloud region, so a failure in one provider affected millions of users across many companies.
items.markingKey: Context (An outage in Amazon Web Services' US-East-1 region disrupted services such as Disney+, Ring doorbells and delivery apps.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: many services relied on the same cloud region, so a failure in one provider affected millions of users across many companies. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interdependence in cloud networks.

items.stem: Using IPv4 exhaustion as an example, explain technical limits shaping access.
items.answer: The pool of unallocated IPv4 addresses held by IANA was exhausted in 2011, and regional registries later ran out; IPv4 addresses are now traded. Scarcity raised costs for new networks, particularly in regions that joined the internet later, while IPv6 adoption remains incomplete.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"This is for everyone."
— Tweet by Tim Berners-Lee displayed during the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony

Explain what the source suggests about the values behind the World Wide Web.
items.answer: The Web was intended to be open and accessible to everyone, free of royalties and gatekeepers – a public resource rather than a private product.
items.markingKey: The Web was intended to be open and accessible to everyone, free of royalties and gatekeepers – a public resource rather than a private product. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A café's Wi-Fi network has a 500 Mbps connection to the internet shared equally by 80 active users. Calculate the bandwidth available to each user, and state whether each user can stream HD video needing 8 Mbps.
items.answer: 6.25 Mbps each; no

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We reject: kings, presidents and voting. We believe in: rough consensus and running code."
— David Clark, Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), 1992

Explain what the source suggests about how internet protocols are developed.
items.answer: Protocols are developed through open, technical consensus among engineers and working implementations, not by governments or votes – a multi-stakeholder, bottom-up process.
items.markingKey: Protocols are developed through open, technical consensus among engineers and working implementations, not by governments or votes – a multi-stakeholder, bottom-up process. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The benefits of the Internet of Things outweigh its risks."
items.answer: Benefits can outweigh risks if devices are secure by design (e.g. the UK PSTI Act 2024 banning default passwords) and data is minimised.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency in energy, transport and health (smart meters, remote monitoring); convenience and accessibility for disabled and elderly users. Arguments against: security weaknesses (Mirai botnet); continuous data collection and surveillance; e-waste from short-lived devices. Supported judgement: Benefits can outweigh risks if devices are secure by design (e.g. the UK PSTI Act 2024 banning default passwords) and data is minimised. items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that cloud computing has made organisations more resilient.
items.answer: The cloud improves resilience for many individual organisations but concentrates systemic risk in a few providers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: redundant data centres and professional security; scales instantly to demand. Arguments against: concentration on a few providers creates single points of failure (AWS 2021, CrowdStrike 2024); dependence on network connectivity; vendor lock-in. Supported judgement: The cloud improves resilience for many individual organisations but concentrates systemic risk in a few providers. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Everyone needs to understand how the internet works to be a responsible digital citizen." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A basic understanding is valuable for safety and civic debate, but secure-by-default design matters more than individual expertise.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: understanding HTTPS, IP addresses and DNS helps avoid scams and protect privacy; informs debates on governance and net neutrality. Arguments against: most users rely on well-designed defaults; responsibility for security lies with providers; basic awareness may be enough. Supported judgement: A basic understanding is valuable for safety and civic debate, but secure-by-default design matters more than individual expertise.
